column1: # Optional keys (a?:1) — dropped from output when unresolved. Columns: name<TAB>mode<TAB>src<TAB>expect
# AN OPTIONAL KEY IS NOT A LIST ELEMENT.
# The decisive argument is Go's own inconsistency, not canonicity: the SAME
# pair without the `?` is discarded by BOTH ports -- `a:[x:1]` is
# `{"a":[]}` everywhere, because a key:value pair is simply not a list
# element. Adding `?` must not turn a discarded pair into a materialised
# one, and in Go it did, purely because the construct reached a different
# The last row is why this matters beyond a stray element: the phantom
# MERGED into a real element, injecting x:1 into {q:9}.
# The same rule with a NUMERIC key (issue #40). This half was divergent
# and invisible: jsonic writes a pair at `node[key]`, and a list's node is
# an array, so a non-numeric key set a property nothing ever read
# (`length` stays 0) while a numeric one set an INDEX and became a real
# element -- TS generated {"a":[1]} for `a:[0:1]` where Go generated
# {"a":[]}, and `a:[1:2]` even filled the gap with a null. That is the
# shape of a JavaScript array, not a decision about the language.
# The last two rows are the ones with teeth: a pair aimed at an index a
# real element already holds must leave that element ALONE, in both
# directions (the pair before the element, and after it).
# An index PAST the end must not grow the list with a hole either.
# The map-level optional key is untouched and must stay that way.
